==English== ===Etymology 1=== {{root|en|ine-pro|*bʰuH-}} From {{inh|en|enm|proven}}, from {{inh|en|ang|prōfian||to esteem, regard as, evince, try, prove}} and {{der|en|fro|prover||to prove}}, both from {{der|en|la|probō||test, try, examine, approve, show to be good or fit, prove|pos=verb}}, from {{m|la|probus||good, worthy, excellent}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*pro-bʰuH-s||being in front, prominent}}, from {{m|ine-pro|*pro-}}, {{m|ine-pro|*per-||toward}} + {{m|ine-pro|*bʰuH-||to be}}. Displaced native {{cog|enm|sothen||to prove}}, from {{cog|ang|sōþian||to prove}}. {{doublet|en|probe}}. More at {{l|en|for}}, {{l|en|be}}, {{l|en|soothe}}. ====Alternative forms==== * {{alt|en|proove||obsolete}} ====Pronunciation==== * {{IPA|en|/ˈpɹuːv/|a=RP}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈpɹʉwv/|a=SSB}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈpɹuv/|a=GA}} ** {{audio|en|en-us-prove.ogg|a=US}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈpɹʉːv/|a=AU,NZ}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈpɾɪʊv/|a=Wales}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈpɾʉv/|a=Scotland}} * {{IPA|en|/ˈpɻʉv/|a=NI}} * {{rhymes|en|uːv|s=1}} * {{hyph|en|prove}} ====Verb==== {{en-verb|+|+|+|+,~n}} # {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[demonstrate]] that something is [[true]] or [[viable]]; to give [[proof]] for; to [[bear out]]; to testify. #: {{syn|en|substantiate}} #* {{quote-book|en|author=Socrates Scholasticus [''i.e.'', {{w|Socrates of Constantinople}}]|chapter=Constantinus the Emperour Summoneth the Nicene Councell, it was Held at Nicæa a Citie of Bythnia for the Debatinge of the Controuersie about the Feast of Easter, and the Rootinge out of the Heresie of Arius|mainauthor=[[w:Eusebius|Eusebius Pamphilus]]; Socrates Scholasticus; w:Evagrius Scholasticus; [[w:Dorotheus of Tyre|Dorotheus]]|tlr=w:Meredith Hanmer|title=The Avncient Ecclesiasticall Histories of the First Six Hundred Yeares after Christ, Wrytten in the Greeke Tongue by Three Learned Historiographers, Eusebius, Socrates, and Euagrius. [...]|location=imprinted at London|publisher=By [[w:Thomas Vautrollier|Thomas Vautroullier]] dwelling in the [[w:Blackfriars|Blackefriers]] by {{w|Ludgate}}|year=1577|volume_plain=book I (The First Booke of the Ecclesiasticall Historye of Socrates Scholasticvs)|page=225|pageurl=https://archive.org/stream/aunciente00euse#page/n224/mode/1up|oclc=55193813|passage=[VV]e are able with playne demonſtration to '''proue''', and vvith reaſon to perſvvade that in tymes paſt our fayth vvas alike, that then vve preached thinges correſpondent vnto the forme of faith already published of vs, ſo that none in this behalfe can repyne or gaynesay vs.}} #* {{RQ:Cleland Fanny Hill|passage=Mr. H …, whom no distinctions of that sort seemed to disturb, scarce gave himself or me breathing time from the last encounter, but, as if he had task'd himself to '''prove''' that the appearances of his vigour were not signs hung out in vain, in a few minutes he was in a condition for renewing the onset}} #* {{quote-journal|en|date=2013-06-07|author=w:Gary Younge|volume=188|issue=26|page=18|magazine=w:The Guardian Weekly |titleurl=http://www.guardian.co.uk/commentisfree/2013/jun/02/hypocrisy-lies-at-heart-bradley-manning-trial|title=Hypocrisy lies at heart of Manning prosecution|passage=WikiLeaks did not cause these uprisings but it certainly informed them. The dispatches revealed details of corruption and kleptocracy that many Tunisians suspected, but could not '''prove''', and would cite as they took to the streets. They also exposed the blatant discrepancy between the west's professed values and actual foreign policies.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20261013134823/https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/jun/02/hypocrisy-lies-at-heart-bradley-manning-trial|archivedate=13 October 2026}} #* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=David Wright|title=Kobach: ‘Election integrity’ panel ‘not set up to prove or to disprove’ Trump|url=https://www.cnn.com/2017/05/15/politics/kris-kobach-new-day-interview-election-integrity-commission-cnntv|date=2017-05-15|passage=“The commission is not set up to disprove or to '''prove''' President Trump’s claim, nor is it just looking at the 2016 election. We’re looking at all forms of election irregularities, voter fraud, voter registration fraud, voter intimidation, suppression, and looking at the vulnerabilities of the various elections we have in each of the 50 states,” Kobach told “New Day” co-host Chris Cuomo.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250828143828/https://www.cnn.com/2017/05/15/politics/kris-kobach-new-day-interview-election-integrity-commission-cnntv|archivedate=28 August 2025}} #* {{quote-book|en|title=Designing Small Evaluation Studies|page=302|author={{w|Larry V. Hedges}}, {{w|Elizabeth Tipton}}|year=2025|passage=Importantly, the hypothesis cannot be '''proven''' to be true—it can only be '''proven''' to be false.}} #: {{ux|en|I will '''prove''' that my method is more effective than yours.}} # {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[turn out]]; to [[manifest]]. #: {{ux|en|It '''proved''' to be a cold day.}} #: {{ux|en|A faulty connection '''proved''' to be the culprit.}} # {{lb|en|copulative}} To [[turn out]] to be. #: {{ux|en|Have an exit strategy should your calculations '''prove''' incorrect.}} #: {{ux|en|The hope that he’d react '''proved''' utterly unfounded.}} #* {{RQ:Marlowe Tamburlaine|part=1|scene=ii|page=27|passage=But ſhall I '''prooue''' a traitor to my King?}} #* '''1964''', [[w:Jean Merrill|Jean Merrill]], [[w:The Pushcart War|''The Pushcart War'']], 2014 [[w:The New York Review Children's Collection|The New York Review Children's Collection]] edition, {{ISBN|9781590178195}}, chapter 33, page 199: # {{lb|en|transitive}} To put to the [[test]], to make trial of. #: {{ux|en|They took the experimental car to the '''proving'''-grounds.}} #: {{ux|en|The exception '''proves''' the rule.}} #* {{RQ:Shakespeare Sonnets|26|text=Then may I dare to boast how I do love thee,
Till then not show my head where thou may'st '''prove''' me.}} #* {{RQ:Scott Tales of the Crusaders|volume=I|chapter=IV|page=71|passage=Wounded and overthrown, the Britons continued their resistance, clung round the legs of the Norman steeds, and cumbered their advance; while their brethren, thrusting with pikes, '''proved''' every joint and crevice of the plate and mail, or grappling with the men-at-arms, strove to pull them from their horses by main force, or beat them down with their bills and Welch hooks.}} # {{lb|en|transitive}} To ascertain or establish the genuineness or validity of; to verify. #: {{co|en|to '''prove''' a will}} # {{lb|en|archaic|transitive}} To [[experience]]. #* {{RQ:Spenser Faerie Queene|book=IV|canto=VI|stanza=34|passage=Where she, captived long, great woes did '''prove'''.}} # {{lb|en|printing|dated|transitive}} To take a [[trial]] [[impression]] of; to take a [[proof]] of. #: ''to '''prove''' a page'' # {{alt form|en|proof||allow (dough) to rise; test the activeness of (yeast); pressure-test (a firearm)}}. # {{lb|en|homeopathy}} To determine by [[experiment]] which [[effect]]s a [[substance]] causes when [[ingest]]ed. =====Usage notes===== Although {{m|en|proven}} is occasionally regarded as less formal than proved as the past participle of {{m|en|proved}}—as in the preference for “have proved” over “have proven”—the two forms are now roughly equally prevalent in American English and are both accepted in British English. While "proved" is more common{{R:Lexico|prove}}{{R:American Heritage 2000|prove}}{{R:Merriam Webster Online|prove}} in British usage, the fixed expression “innocent until proven guilty” remains standard, whereas “innocent until proved guilty” is comparatively rare. In addition, as an attributive adjective, ''proven'' is much more commonly used, and {{m|en|proved}} is widely proscribed – “a proven method”, not “a proved method”. Historically, ''proved'' is the older form, while ''proven'' arose as a Scottish variant – see [[proven#Etymology|etymology]]. Used in legal writing from the mid-17th century, it entered literary usage more slowly, only becoming significant in the 19th century, with the poet {{w|Alfred, Lord Tennyson}}, among the earliest frequent users (presumably for reasons of meter). In the 19th century, ''proven'' was widely discouraged, and remained significantly less common through the mid-20th century (''proved'' being used approximately four times as often); by the late 20th century it came to be used about equally often in US English. =====Conjugation===== {{en-conj|stem=prov|old=1|past_ptc2=proven}} =====Derived terms===== {{col|en|unproving |counterprove|misprove|overprove|reprove |disprovability |disprovable |disprovably |disprove |disproved |disproven |exception that proves the rule |fend and prove|prove oneself |provability |provable |provably |prove out |prover |proving ground |unprovability |unprovable |unprovably |unprove |unproved |unproven |until proven otherwise}} =====Related terms===== {{col4|en |approve |probe |probity |proof }} =====Translations===== {{trans-top-see|to demonstrate that something is true; David McGuinness|title=Bourke Street Bakery: the ultimate baking companion |passage=You may also need to think about what the '''prove''' is doing to the loaf of bread — it is warming the dough and making it moist, allowing it to rise {{...}}}} ===Etymology 2=== Simple past form of {{m|en|proove}}, conjugated as a Germanic [[strong verb]], on the pattern of {{m|en|choose}} → {{m|en|chose}}. ====Pronunciation==== * {{IPA|en|/pɹəʊv/|a=RP}} ====Verb==== {{head|en|verb form}} # {{infl of|en|proove||spast}} ===Further reading=== * {{R:OneLook}} * {{R:Webster 1913}} * {{R:Century}} ===Anagrams=== * {{anagrams|en|a=eoprv|Prevo|pervo}} {{cln|en|raising verbs|irregular verbs|verbs with weak preterite but strong past participle}}
